A 21.8 mg sorbent 2 sample underwent a 4-h adsorption phase, followed by a 2-h desorption phase using N at 100°C. 2 Figure 32A presents the schematic of the adsorption bed setup in Aspen Adsorption, while Figure 32B illustrates the CO₂ loading profile of the sorbent over time. Table 6 gives the details of the simulation specifications of the bed as setup on aspen adsorption. As shown, the CO₂ loading capacity reaches approximately 3.9 mmol/g by the end of the 4-h adsorption phase, and complete desorption is achieved within the subsequent 2-h desorption period. The CO₂ loading capacity curve was obtained for the sorbent positioned at the center of the bed. After several iterations, the best-fit breakthrough curve data were recorded, as shown in Figure 32C, aligning well with the sorbent capacity measured in the laboratory. Figure 32. Scaling up Bed Using Aspen Adsorption Aspen Adsorption was used to scale up the adsorption bed by increasing both the sample size and bed dimensions, while maintaining a constant bed aspect ratio (length-to-diameter) and packing density. The airflow rate was proportionally increased with the sorbent mass, ensuring consistent CO₂ and water vapor concentrations. All other parameters, including adsorption isotherms and mass transfer coefficients, were kept constant. As shown in Figure 33A, the breakthrough curve exhibits slight variations due to changes in sorbent exposure and bed pressure dynamics. However, the maximum sorbent loading remains consistent, as illustrated in Figure 33B. Figure 33. Breakthrough curve (A) and sorbent loading results for bed scaling up using Aspen Adsorption.
